chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text: A force is a push or a pull exerted on an object due to interaction with another object. Force has both magnitude and direction.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Force arises due to the interaction between two objects.
Force has magnitude as well as direction.
A change in speed, direction of motion, or both is called a change in state of motion.
Force acting on an object may cause a change in its state of motion or a change in its shape.
Force can act on an object with or without being in contact with it.
Force per unit area is called pressure.
Liquids and gases exert pressure on the walls of their containers.
The pressure exerted by air around us is known as atmospheric pressure.

items.question: What is a force? Give two examples.
items.answer:
A force is a push or a pull exerted on an object due to interaction with another object.
Examples: Kicking a football (push), drawing water from a well (pull).

items.question: State two effects of force on an object.
items.answer:
1. Force may change the state of motion of an object (make it move, stop, or change direction).
2. Force may change the shape of an object.

items.question: Distinguish between contact forces and non-contact forces with one example each.
items.answer:
Contact forces act only when the agent is in contact with the object.
Example: Muscular force - pushing a table.
Non-contact forces can act without physical contact between objects.
Example: Magnetic force - a magnet attracting iron filings from a distance.

items.question: What is pressure? Write its formula and explain why sharp tools cut better than blunt ones.
items.answer:
Pressure is the force acting on a unit area of a surface.
FORMULA: Pressure = Force / Area on which it acts
Sharp tools have a very small area at their edge, so the same force produces a much greater pressure. Blunt tools have a larger area, producing less pressure for the same force. Hence sharp tools cut more easily.

items.question: Explain the three effects of force on a moving object with examples.
items.answer:
1. A force in the direction of motion increases the speed of the object.
Example: A player pushing a rolling ball in the same direction makes it go faster.
2. A force opposite to the direction of motion decreases the speed of the object.
Example: A goalkeeper applying force to stop a moving ball reduces its speed to zero.
3. A force at an angle to the direction of motion changes the direction of the object.
Example: A batsman hitting a ball with a bat changes the ball's direction.

items.question: What is atmospheric pressure? How does the rubber sucker activity demonstrate its magnitude?
items.answer:
Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the air (atmosphere) surrounding us on all objects.
The atmosphere is an envelope of air extending many kilometres above the earth's surface. Pressure = Force / Area, and the force here is the weight of the column of air above a unit area.
Rubber sucker activity: When a rubber sucker is pressed hard on a smooth surface, most air between the cup and the surface escapes. The atmospheric pressure then acts on the outer surface of the sucker, pressing it firmly against the surface. It requires a very large force to pull the sucker off because atmospheric pressure is very large - equivalent to the weight of a 225 kg object pressing on a 15 cm x 15 cm area of a person's head.

items.question: Describe all the ways in which a force can affect an object. Support each with an activity or example from the chapter.
items.answer:
A force can affect an object in the following ways:

1. MAKES A STATIONARY OBJECT MOVE:
A stationary object begins to move when a force is applied on it.
Example (Activity 8.3): A rubber ball placed on a level surface begins to move when gently pushed.

2. CHANGES SPEED OF A MOVING OBJECT:
If force is applied in the direction of motion, speed increases. If force is applied opposite to motion, speed decreases.
Example: A goalkeeper diving to stop a ball applies a force that reduces the ball's speed to zero.

3. CHANGES DIRECTION OF A MOVING OBJECT:
A force applied at an angle to the direction of motion changes the direction.
Example (Activity 8.4): A ball rolling on a surface changes direction when it strikes a ruler placed in its path.

4. CHANGES SHAPE OF AN OBJECT:
When force is applied on an object that cannot move freely, it changes the object's shape.
Example (Activity 8.5): Pressing a lump of dough, stretching a rubber band, pressing a spring - all demonstrate change in shape.

5. MAY HAVE NO EFFECT:
Sometimes applying a force does not result in any change - for example, pushing a wall.

topics.topic_name: FORCE - A PUSH OR A PULL

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: A force is a push or a pull. In science, a push or a pull on an object is called a force. The motion imparted to objects is due to the action of a force.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Actions like picking, opening, shutting, kicking, hitting, lifting, flicking, pushing, pulling are often used to describe certain tasks.
Each of these actions results in some kind of change in the state of motion of an object.
All these actions can be replaced with the terms PUSH or PULL (or both).
When does a force come into play? A force comes into play when an object is pushed or pulled.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.1:
sections.aim:
To identify actions involving push and/or pull in familiar situations.
TABLE 8.1: IDENTIFYING ACTIONS AS PUSH OR PULL
Situations given: Moving a book on a table, Opening/shutting a door, Drawing a bucket from a well, A footballer taking a penalty kick, A cricket ball hit by a batsman, Moving a loaded cart, Opening a drawer.
sections.observation: Each action can be grouped as a push, a pull, or both.
sections.conclusion:
To move an object, it has to be pushed or pulled.

KEY TERMS:
FORCE - a push or a pull on an object
PUSH - a force applied away from the body/agent
PULL - a force applied towards the body/agent

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is a force in science? Give two everyday examples.
items.answer:
In science, a push or a pull on an object is called a force.
Examples: Pushing a door to close it; pulling a drawer to open it.

items.question: From Activity 8.1, what do you conclude about moving an object?
items.answer: From Activity 8.1, we conclude that to move an object (or change its state of motion), it has to be either pushed or pulled. Both pushing and pulling involve the application of a force.

items.question: List any four actions from daily life and identify each as a push, a pull, or both.
items.answer:
1. Opening a door - Pull (towards us) or Push (away from us) depending on direction.
2. Drawing water from a well - Pull (rope pulled upward).
3. A footballer kicking a ball - Push (foot pushes ball away).
4. Moving a loaded cart - Push (person pushes cart forward).

items.question: Can the terms push and pull replace all the actions described in Table 8.1? Justify with two examples.
items.answer:
Yes, all the actions in Table 8.1 can be replaced with push or pull (or both).
Example 1: Moving a book on a table involves both pushing (forward) and pulling (towards oneself) - it can be classified under both.
Example 2: A football player taking a penalty kick applies a push on the stationary ball, making it move.
Thus, all actions that result in a change in state of motion can be described as a push or a pull, confirming that these two terms adequately replace all such action words.

items.question: What is a force? Explain with reference to Activity 8.1 how we come to know that force involves a push or a pull.
items.answer:
A force is a push or a pull exerted on an object.
In Activity 8.1, students are asked to examine familiar situations such as opening a door, drawing a bucket from a well, a footballer kicking a ball, and a batsman hitting a cricket ball.
For each situation, students identify whether the action is a push, a pull, or both:
- Drawing a bucket = Pull (upward force on rope).
- Kicking a ball = Push (foot exerts force on ball away from body).
- Moving a loaded cart = Push (person exerts force on cart away from body).
From this activity, we conclude that all everyday actions that change the state of motion of an object involve either a push or a pull - both of which are forces. This establishes that a force is fundamentally a push or a pull.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.1 and state its observation and conclusion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.1 - Identifying Actions as Push or Pull:
sections.observation: Every action listed in the table can be identified as a push, a pull, or both. No action falls outside these two categories.
sections.conclusion:
To move an object (or change its state of motion), it must be either pushed or pulled. Thus, all such actions involve the application of a force.

Q7[6 Marks] What is force? With the help of Table 8.1 (Activity 8.1), explain how everyday actions involving motion can all be classified as push or pull. Also state why force is considered a fundamental concept in science.
A7:

sections.label: DEFINITION OF FORCE:
sections.text: In science, a push or a pull on an object is called a force. The motion imparted to objects is due to the action of a force.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.1 AND TABLE 8.1:
sections.observation: In every case, the action results in some change in the state of motion of the object. Every such action is either a push, a pull, or a combination of both.
sections.conclusion:
All actions that move objects or change their state of motion are fundamentally pushes or pulls. The terms push and pull together describe ALL forces encountered in everyday life.

WHY FORCE IS FUNDAMENTAL:
Force is the underlying cause of all changes in motion. Without a force, no object can change its speed or direction. Understanding force as a push or pull helps us analyze every physical interaction - from picking a pencil to launching a rocket - in terms of this single concept.

topics.topic_name: FORCES ARE DUE TO AN INTERACTION

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: An interaction of one object with another results in a force between the two objects. At least two objects must be present for a force to come into play.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A stationary car does not move just because a person stands behind it; the person must apply a force (push) on it.
In Fig. 8.2(a): Man standing behind stationary car - car does not move.
In Fig. 8.2(b): Man pushes car - car begins to move in the direction of the applied force.
In Fig. 8.3: Two girls pushing each other (push), two girls pulling each other (pull), a man and a cow pulling each other (pull) - in all cases, at least two objects are interacting.
An interaction of one object with another object results in a force between the two objects.
Both objects in an interaction experience force; when you push a wall, the wall also pushes back on you.
KEY TERMS:
INTERACTION - the mutual action or influence between two objects
FORCE - the result of an interaction between two objects

items.question: Why does a stationary car not move when a man simply stands behind it?
items.answer: A stationary car does not move when a man simply stands behind it because the man is not applying any force on the car. There is no interaction (push or pull) between the man and the car. A force comes into play only when the man begins to push the car.

items.question: What is the minimum requirement for a force to come into play?
items.answer: At least two objects must be present and there must be an interaction between them for a force to come into play. A single isolated object cannot experience a force.

items.question: Explain with the example of Fig. 8.3 that an interaction between two objects results in a force.
items.answer:
Fig. 8.3 shows three situations:
(a) Two girls appear to push each other - each is exerting a push force on the other.
(b) Two girls try to pull each other - each exerts a pull force on the other.
(c) A man and a cow appear to pull each other - each exerts a pull on the other.
In each case, there is an interaction between two objects (the two girls, or the man and the cow). This interaction results in a force on each object. This confirms that an interaction of one object with another results in a force between the two objects.

items.question: A man pushes a car. Who exerts force on whom? Is it only the man who exerts force?
items.answer:
When a man pushes a car, the man exerts a push force on the car (from behind, in the forward direction). This is due to the interaction between the man and the car.
However, according to Newton's Third Law (which we observe in everyday life), the car also exerts an equal and opposite force back on the man (a reaction force pushes the man backward).
So it is not only the man who exerts force - both objects (the man and the car) exert forces on each other due to their interaction.

items.question: Using examples from Fig. 8.2 and Fig. 8.3, explain that forces arise due to interactions between two objects.
items.answer:
Fig. 8.2 example:
(a) A man merely stands behind a stationary car. There is no interaction (no push/pull). The car does not move.
(b) The same man begins to push the car. Now there is a direct interaction between the man and the car. The car begins to move in the direction of the applied force.
This shows that a force only arises when there is an active interaction.

Fig. 8.3 examples:
(a) Two girls appear to push each other - interaction exists between the two girls, resulting in push forces on each other.
(b) Two girls try to pull each other - interaction results in pull forces on each other.
(c) A man and a cow pull each other - interaction results in pull forces on both.

CONCLUSION: In all these examples, a force only exists when two objects interact. The interaction of one object with another results in a force between the two objects. A single isolated object cannot experience a force.

items.question: What do you understand by "forces arise due to interaction"? Explain with two examples from everyday life.
items.answer:
The statement "forces arise due to interaction" means that a force always requires at least two objects to be present, and there must be a mutual action between them.

Example 1: A person pushing a shopping cart
The person's hands interact with the cart by pushing it. This interaction produces a force on the cart (in the direction of the push) and an equal and opposite force on the person's hands (pushing back). Without the interaction, no force exists.

Example 2: Tug-of-war
Two teams pull at a rope. Team A interacts with the rope by pulling it in one direction; Team B interacts with the rope by pulling it in the opposite direction. Each team exerts a force on the rope due to this interaction. If both forces are equal, the rope does not move - this also demonstrates that forces have both magnitude and direction.

CONCLUSION: In every case, a force arises only because two objects are interacting with each other. An interaction of one object with another always results in a force between the two objects.

items.question: Explain in detail, using figures and examples from the chapter, that "an interaction of one object with another object results in a force between the two objects." Also explain what happens when two forces act on an object in the same direction and in opposite directions.
items.answer:
FORCES ARISE DUE TO INTERACTION:
A force cannot exist in isolation. It always involves two objects interacting with each other.

From Fig. 8.2:
(a) Man standing behind a stationary car - no interaction, no force, car remains at rest.
(b) Man pushes the car - interaction begins, force is applied, car starts to move.
This shows that interaction is necessary for force to arise.

From Fig. 8.3:
Three situations show pairs of objects interacting:
(a) Two girls pushing each other - push force on each due to interaction.
(b) Two girls pulling each other - pull force on each due to interaction.
(c) Man and cow pulling each other - pull force on each due to interaction.
In all three cases, a force appears only because two objects interact.

FORCES IN THE SAME DIRECTION:
When two forces act on an object in the same direction, they ADD to each other.
Example (Activity 8.2): When two people push a heavy box in the same direction, it is easier to move than when one person pushes alone. The net force = sum of both forces.

FORCES IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS:
When two forces act on an object in opposite directions, the net force is the DIFFERENCE between the two forces.
Example: In tug-of-war (Fig. 8.5), if both teams pull with equal force, the net force is zero and the rope does not move. If one team pulls harder, the net force is in that team's direction, and the rope moves toward them.

MAGNITUDE AND DIRECTION:
The strength of a force is expressed by its MAGNITUDE. Force also has a direction - the direction in which the push or pull acts. If either the magnitude or the direction of an applied force changes, its effect also changes.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The magnitude of a force is its strength. Forces have both magnitude and direction. When forces act in the same direction they add up; when they act in opposite directions the net force is the difference between them.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Force has magnitude (strength) and direction.
Forces applied in the same direction ADD to one another (net force = sum of both).
Forces applied in opposite directions: the net force is the DIFFERENCE between the two forces, acting in the direction of the larger force.
If two equal and opposite forces act on an object, the net force is zero and the object does not move.
In general, more than one force may be acting on an object; the effect is due to the NET force.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.2:
sections.aim: To explore how direction of forces affects an object's motion.
sections.materials: A heavy object (table or box).
procedure: Step 1: Push the heavy object all by yourself. Note whether it moves.
Step 2: Ask a friend to push in the SAME direction. Note whether it moves and whether it is easier.
Step 3: Now ask the friend to push from the OPPOSITE side. Observe the direction the object moves.
sections.observation:
- Two people pushing in the same direction: object moves more easily; the force is larger.
- Two people pushing in opposite directions: the object may not move, or moves in the direction of the larger force.
sections.conclusion:
Forces in the same direction add to each other. Forces in opposite directions subtract from each other. The net force and its direction determine the motion of the object.

KEY TERMS:
MAGNITUDE - the strength or size of a force
NET FORCE - the resultant force obtained by combining all forces acting on an object

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is the magnitude of a force?
items.answer: The magnitude of a force is the measure of its strength or size. A force with greater magnitude produces a larger effect on an object. The unit of force is Newton (N). Magnitude tells us HOW LARGE a force is, while direction tells us WHERE it acts.

items.question: What happens to the net force when two forces act on an object in the same direction?
items.answer: When two forces act on an object in the same direction, the net force is equal to the SUM of the two forces. This makes the combined force greater than either force alone, and the object moves more easily in that direction.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.2 and state what it tells us about forces.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.2:
procedure: 1: One person tries to push it alone - it may not move or moves with difficulty.
Step 2: A friend helps push in the SAME direction - the object moves more easily. The two forces add up.
Step 3: The friend pushes from the OPPOSITE side - both push with equal force. The object does not move. If one pushes harder, the object moves in the direction of the stronger push.
sections.conclusion:
The net force determines whether an object moves, how fast it moves, and in which direction it moves. Just knowing one force is not enough - we must consider ALL forces and their directions to predict the motion of an object.

Q6[4 Marks] What do you understand by "a force has magnitude and direction"? Support with examples from the chapter.
A6:
Every force has two important properties:

1. MAGNITUDE - the strength or size of the force:
A small push moves a light object; a large push is needed to move a heavy object. The magnitude tells us HOW MUCH force is applied.
Example: In Activity 8.2, one person pushing a heavy box cannot move it (force too small), but two people pushing together (greater combined magnitude) succeed in moving it.

2. DIRECTION - the line along which the force acts:
The direction of the force determines where the object will move.
Example 1: Two people pushing a box in the SAME direction - box moves in that direction with increased force.
Example 2: Two people pushing from OPPOSITE sides - if forces are equal, box does not move (net force = 0, no definite direction).

If either the magnitude or direction of an applied force changes, its effect on the object also changes.
Example: A goalkeeper can stop a ball (force opposite to ball's motion decreases its speed) or deflect it (force at an angle changes direction). Both outcomes depend on the magnitude and direction of the applied force.

Q7[6 Marks] Describe in detail Activity 8.2. Explain what happens when two forces act in the same direction and in opposite directions on an object. Use the tug-of-war example to illustrate your explanation.
A7:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.2 - Exploring Forces:
sections.materials: A heavy table or box.
procedure: Step 1: One person tries to push the heavy object alone. It may not move, or moves with difficulty.
Step 2: A friend is asked to push the same object from the SAME side (same direction). Both push together. The object moves more easily.

Step 3: The same friend is now asked to push from the OPPOSITE side (pushing against the first person's push). Both push with similar effort. Observe whether the object moves, and if so, in which direction.
sections.observation:
- Same direction: Object moves easily. Net force = sum of both individual forces.
- Opposite direction (approximately equal): Object does not move. Net force approaches zero.
- Opposite direction (one stronger): Object moves toward the side with the larger force.
sections.conclusion:
Forces in the same direction ADD, making the net force larger. Forces in opposite directions SUBTRACT, reducing the net force.

TUG-OF-WAR EXAMPLE (Fig. 8.5):
Two teams pull a rope in opposite directions.
- If Team A pulls harder: rope moves toward Team A. Net force = Force by A - Force by B (in Team A's direction).
- If both teams pull equally: rope does not move. Net force = 0.
- The team applying the LARGER force wins, because the net force is in their direction.

GENERAL PRINCIPLE:
The effect on an object depends on the NET force acting on it.
- Net force = Sum of all forces (taking direction into account).
- The direction of net force determines the direction of motion.
- The magnitude of net force determines the acceleration or change in speed.
The strength of a force is expressed by its magnitude, and its effect depends on both magnitude and direction.

topics.topic_name: A FORCE CAN CHANGE THE STATE OF MOTION

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and the direction of motion. The state of rest is considered to be the state of zero speed. A force may bring about a change in the state of motion of an object.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A force applied on an object may change its speed.
If force is in the direction of motion - speed INCREASES.
If force is opposite to direction of motion - speed DECREASES.
A force can also change the direction of motion of an object.
A change in either speed or direction of motion (or both) is called a CHANGE IN STATE OF MOTION.
A force may bring about a change in the state of motion of an object.
Application of a force does NOT always result in a change in state of motion (e.g., pushing a wall - no effect).
An object cannot move by itself, change speed by itself, change direction by itself, or change shape by itself - a force is always needed.
STATE OF MOTION:
The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and the direction of motion.
The state of rest is the state of zero speed.
An object may be at rest or in motion; both are its states of motion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.3:
sections.aim: To observe how force changes the state of motion of a ball.
sections.materials: Rubber ball, level surface (table top or concrete floor).
procedure: Step 1: Place a rubber ball on a level surface. Gently push it. Does it move?
Step 2: Push the ball again while it is still moving. Does its speed increase or decrease?
Step 3: Place your palm in front of the moving ball. Remove the palm as soon as the ball touches it. Does the palm apply force? What happens to the ball's speed?
Step 4: Hold the moving ball with your palm. What happens to its speed?
sections.observation:
- Ball begins to move when pushed (from rest to motion).
- Speed increases when pushed again while moving.
- Palm briefly touching ball slightly decreases its speed.
- Holding ball with palm stops it completely (speed becomes zero).
sections.conclusion: A force applied on a ball can make it move from rest, increase its speed, decrease its speed, or bring it to rest. Force changes the state of motion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.4:
sections.aim: To observe that force can change the direction of motion of an object.
sections.materials: Rubber ball, ruler, level surface.
procedure: Step 1: Set a ball in motion by pushing it along a level surface.
Step 2: Place a ruler in its path at an angle. Note the direction of the ball's motion after it hits the ruler.
Step 3: Repeat by placing the ruler at different angles.
sections.observation: The ball changes direction after striking the ruler at different angles. The new direction depends on the angle at which the ruler is placed.
sections.conclusion: A force (applied by the ruler on the ball) can change the direction of motion of a moving object.

sections.label: DO YOU KNOW BOX (STATE OF MOTION):
sections.text:
The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and the direction of motion. The state of rest is considered to be the state of zero speed. An object may be at rest or in motion; both are its states of motion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is meant by the "state of motion" of an object?
items.answer: The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and the direction of motion. The state of rest is the state of zero speed. An object may be at rest or in motion - both are considered its states of motion.

items.question: A goalkeeper dives to stop a ball. How does the force applied by the goalkeeper affect the ball?
items.answer: The ball is moving at high speed toward the goal. The goalkeeper applies a force on the ball in the direction OPPOSITE to the ball's motion. This force reduces the ball's speed. If the goalkeeper succeeds, the ball's speed decreases to zero - it stops completely. The force has changed the state of motion of the ball from moving to rest.

items.question: What is a "change in state of motion"? Give two examples.
items.answer:
A change in either the speed of an object, or the direction of its motion, or both, is called a change in its state of motion.
Example 1 (change in speed): A stationary ball begins to move when kicked. Its speed changes from zero to some value. This is a change in state of motion.
Example 2 (change in direction): A hockey player flicks a moving ball with a stick, changing its direction of travel without significantly changing its speed. The direction changed, so the state of motion changed.

items.question: Does the application of a force always result in a change in state of motion? Justify your answer.
items.answer:
No, the application of a force does NOT always result in a change in state of motion.
Example 1: When you try to push a heavy wall, you apply force, but the wall does not move. No change in state of motion occurs.
Example 2: When you try to push a very heavy box beyond your capacity, the box does not move despite the force applied.
This is because in many cases, other forces (like friction or the structural strength of the object) oppose the applied force, and the net force remains zero or insufficient to produce motion. While a force may cause a change in state of motion, it does not always guarantee one.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.3 and explain how it demonstrates that force can change the state of motion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.3 - Force Changing State of Motion:
sections.materials: Rubber ball, level surface.
procedure: Step 1: Place a rubber ball on a level surface. Gently push it. The ball begins to move - a stationary object has started moving due to force.
Step 2: Push the ball again while it is still moving (in the same direction). The ball moves faster - speed has increased due to force in the direction of motion.
Step 3: Place your palm in front of the moving ball and remove it quickly when the ball touches. The ball's speed slightly decreases - force opposite to motion has slowed it.
Step 4: Hold the moving ball firmly with your palm. The ball stops - speed reduces to zero due to force applied opposite to its motion.
sections.observation:
S:
- Ball moved from rest when pushed (speed: 0 to some value).
- Ball moved faster when pushed again (speed increased).
- Ball slowed when palm touched it briefly (speed decreased).
- Ball stopped when palm held it (speed decreased to zero).
sections.conclusion:
In each step, the application of a force changed the state of motion of the ball - either by starting motion, increasing speed, decreasing speed, or stopping the ball. This proves that force can change the state of motion of an object.

Q6[4 Marks] Describe Activity 8.4. What does it show about the effect of force on direction of motion?
A6:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.4 - Force Changing Direction of Motion:
sections.materials: Rubber ball, ruler (as an obstacle), level surface.
procedure: Step 1: Give the ball a push on the level surface so it rolls forward.
Step 2: Place a ruler in its path (at right angles or at various angles) so that the ball strikes the ruler.
Step 3: Note the direction in which the ball moves after striking the ruler.
Step 4: Repeat by placing the ruler at different angles to the ball's path.
sections.observation: After striking the ruler, the ball bounces off and moves in a different direction. Changing the angle of the ruler changes the new direction of the ball's motion.
sections.conclusion:
The ruler exerts a force on the moving ball when the ball strikes it. This force changes the direction of the ball's motion. The application of a force (here by the ruler) can change the direction of a moving object. This shows that a force can change the state of motion of an object by changing its direction.

Q7[6 Marks] Explain all the possible effects of force on a moving object, using activities and real-life examples from Chapter 8.
A7:
A force applied on a moving object can have the following effects:

1. INCREASE IN SPEED (force in direction of motion):
If a force acts on an object in the same direction as its motion, the speed of the object increases.
Example (Activity 8.3, Step 2): Pushing a rolling ball in the direction it is already moving increases its speed.
Real-life example: A player pushing a rolling tyre repeatedly - each push makes it go faster (as noted by Paheli in the Do you know box, Fig. 8.7).

2. DECREASE IN SPEED (force opposite to direction of motion):
If a force acts on an object in the direction OPPOSITE to its motion, the speed decreases.
Example (Activity 8.3, Step 3 and 4): Placing a palm to oppose the moving ball reduces its speed. Holding the ball stops it.
Real-life example: In football, before taking a penalty kick, the ball is at rest. The goalkeeper dives and applies a force on the ball. The force opposite to the ball's motion reduces its speed to zero.

3. CHANGE IN DIRECTION OF MOTION:
A force applied at an angle to the direction of motion changes the direction.
Example (Activity 8.4): A ball rolling on a surface strikes a ruler placed at an angle and bounces off in a new direction.
Real-life example (Activity 8.4 note): In volleyball, players push the moving ball to their teammates - changing its direction. In cricket, a batsman hits the ball with a bat, changing both its speed and direction.

4. CHANGE IN BOTH SPEED AND DIRECTION:
Force can simultaneously change both speed and direction of a moving object.
Real-life example: A batsman hits a fast-pitched ball and the ball changes both its speed (slows down and comes back) and direction (now goes in a different direction after the shot).

5. NO CHANGE IN STATE OF MOTION:
Sometimes a force is applied but no change occurs.
Example: Pushing a wall - force is applied, but the wall does not move and its state of motion does not change.

GENERAL CONCLUSION:
A change in speed, direction of motion, or both is called a change in the state of motion of an object. Thus, a force may bring about a change in the state of motion of an object. However, the application of a force does not always guarantee a change - it depends on the net force and the resistance of the object.

topics.topic_name: FORCE CAN CHANGE THE SHAPE OF AN OBJECT

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: When a force is applied on an object that is not free to move, the force may change the shape of the object instead of changing its state of motion.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A force can change the shape of an object.
Objects that cannot move freely undergo a change in shape when force is applied.
Examples: pressing dough, squeezing a rubber ball, stretching a rubber band, bending a metal scale.
Summary of effects of force: a force may make an object move from rest, change speed if moving, change direction of moving object, change shape of object, or cause some or all of these effects.
IMPORTANT: None of these effects can take place without the action of a force. An object cannot move by itself, stop by itself, change direction by itself, or change shape by itself.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.5:
sections.aim:
To observe the effect of force on the shape of different objects.
TABLE 8.2: STUDYING THE EFFECT OF FORCE ON OBJECTS
Situations:
1. A lump of dough on a plate - press it down with hands.
2. A spring fixed to the seat of a bicycle - sit on the seat.
3. A rubber band suspended from a hook/nail - hang a weight or pull its free end.
4. A plastic or metal scale placed between two bricks - put a weight at the centre of the scale.

For each situation: note whether there is a Change in State of Motion (Yes/No) and Change in Shape (Yes/No).
sections.observation:
- Lump of dough: Cannot move freely. No change in state of motion. CHANGE IN SHAPE (Yes) - dough flattens.
- Bicycle spring: Fixed to seat. No change in state of motion. CHANGE IN SHAPE (Yes) - spring compresses.
- Rubber band: Stretched by weight. CHANGE IN SHAPE (Yes) - rubber band elongates.
- Metal/plastic scale: Fixed at ends. CHANGE IN SHAPE (Yes) - scale bends in the middle.
sections.conclusion:
When force is applied on objects that are not free to move, the force causes a change in shape. Thus, force can change the shape of an object.

SUMMARY OF EFFECTS OF FORCE (from Activity 8.5):
A force applied on an object may:
- Make it move from rest.
- Change its speed if already moving.
- Change the direction of its motion.
- Bring about a change in its shape.
- Cause some or all of the above effects.
IMPORTANT NOTE: None of these actions can take place without the action of a force. An object cannot move by itself, change speed by itself, change direction by itself, or change shape by itself.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Give two examples where force changes the shape of an object.
items.answer:
1. Pressing a lump of dough with your hands: The dough cannot move (fixed on plate), so the force changes its shape - it flattens out.
2. Stretching a rubber band: Pulling the free end of a rubber band hung from a nail elongates it, changing its shape.

items.question: Why does pressing a lump of dough change its shape but not its state of motion?
items.answer: A lump of dough on a plate is not free to move freely because it is on a surface and being pressed down. When force is applied (pressing down), the dough cannot move in that direction (the plate provides resistance). Since the dough cannot move, the applied force instead causes a CHANGE IN SHAPE - the dough flattens. There is no change in state of motion (it remains at rest), but its shape changes.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.5 and write its observations and conclusion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.5 - Effect of Force on Shape:
sections.observation:
S (from Table 8.2):
- Dough: Change in State of Motion = No. Change in Shape = Yes (flattens).
- Bicycle spring: Change in State of Motion = No. Change in Shape = Yes (compresses).
- Rubber band: Change in State of Motion = No. Change in Shape = Yes (elongates).
- Metal scale: Change in State of Motion = No. Change in Shape = Yes (bends).
sections.conclusion:
When objects are not free to move, force applied on them brings about a change in their shape. Force can change the shape of an object.

Q4[3 Marks] Summarise all the effects of force on an object as given at the end of Topic 8.5.
A4:
A force applied on an object may bring about one or more of the following effects:
1. It may make the object move from rest (start motion).
2. It may change the speed of a moving object (increase or decrease speed).
3. It may change the direction of motion of a moving object.
4. It may change the shape of an object (if it cannot move freely).
5. It may cause some or all of the above effects simultaneously.
IMPORTANT: None of these effects can take place without the action of a force. An object cannot move by itself, change speed by itself, change direction by itself, or change shape by itself.

Q5[4 Marks] What happens to the shape of a rubber band when a weight is hung from it? What does this tell us about force?
A5:
When a rubber band is suspended from a hook/nail fixed on a wall (as in Activity 8.5), and a weight is hung from its free end or the free end is pulled down:
- The rubber band STRETCHES (elongates) - it becomes longer than its original length.
- This is a change in SHAPE of the rubber band.
- If the weight is removed, the rubber band returns to its original shape (elastic property).

WHAT THIS TELLS US ABOUT FORCE:
1. Force can change the shape of an object - the gravitational force (weight) hanging from the rubber band has changed its shape by stretching it.
2. The rubber band is fixed at one end (hung from a nail) and cannot move freely, so the force causes shape change instead of motion.
3. The amount of stretch (change in shape) depends on the MAGNITUDE of the force applied - heavier weight = more stretch.
4. When the force is removed, the rubber band returns to its original shape, showing that the shape change was due to the applied force.

Q6[4 Marks] Why is it said that "an object cannot move by itself"? Explain with reference to the effects of force.
A6:
The statement "an object cannot move by itself" means that without the action of an external force, a stationary object remains at rest and a moving object cannot change its speed or direction on its own.

This is based on the observations from the chapter:
1. A rubber ball placed on a level surface does not move by itself (Activity 8.3, Step 1). It moves only when a push is applied.
2. A car does not move by itself even when a man stands behind it (Fig. 8.2a). It moves only when the man pushes it.
3. A stationary lump of dough does not change shape by itself - only when force (pressing) is applied does it flatten.

EFFECTS OF FORCE AND THEIR MEANING:
- Move from rest: Needs a force to start.
- Change speed: Needs a force in the direction of or opposite to motion.
- Change direction: Needs a force at an angle to the motion.
- Change shape: Needs a force applied on the object.

Therefore, for ANY change to occur in an object - whether in its motion, speed, direction, or shape - a FORCE must act on it. Nothing happens "by itself." This is a fundamental principle of physics: an external force is always required to bring about a change in an object.

Q7[6 Marks] Write a comprehensive account of all the effects of force as demonstrated through Activities 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. Include the purpose, key observation, and conclusion of each activity.
A7:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.3 - Force Changing State of Motion (Speed):
sections.conclusion: Force can start motion, increase speed, decrease speed, and stop a moving object. Force changes the state of motion of an object.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.4 - Force Changing Direction of Motion:
sections.conclusion: A force (from the ruler) changes the direction of the ball's motion. Force can change the direction of motion of a moving object. This is also a change in state of motion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.5 - Force Changing Shape of an Object:
sections.conclusion:
Force applied on objects that cannot move freely causes a change in shape. Force can change the shape of an object.

COMPLETE SUMMARY OF EFFECTS OF FORCE:
From all three activities, we can list all possible effects of force:
1. Force can make a stationary object move.
2. Force can increase the speed of a moving object (if applied in direction of motion).
3. Force can decrease the speed of a moving object (if applied opposite to motion).
4. Force can change the direction of motion of an object.
5. Force can change the shape of an object.
6. Force may cause some or all of these effects simultaneously.

IMPORTANT: None of these effects can take place without the action of a force. An object cannot move by itself, change speed by itself, change direction by itself, or change shape by itself. This makes force one of the most fundamental concepts in science.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Contact forces are forces that arise only when the agent applying the force is in physical contact with the object on which the force is applied.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: To apply a force on an object, the body of the agent must generally be in contact with the object.
MUSCULAR FORCE: Force resulting from the action of muscles in our body. It is also called a contact force because muscles must be in contact with an object to exert force.
FRICTION: A contact force that acts in the direction opposite to the motion of a moving object. It always acts on moving objects.
Friction arises because of contact between surfaces.
Muscular force can only be applied when the agent is in contact with the object.
MUSCULAR FORCE:
DEFINITION: The force resulting due to the action of muscles in our body is known as muscular force. It is also called a contact force.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: To push or lift an object, we use muscular force.
Animals also use muscular force for physical activities (bullocks pulling a cart, horses carrying loads, donkeys and camels performing tasks - Fig. 8.9).
Muscular force is used in many body activities: digestion (food pushed through alimentary canal), breathing (lungs expanding and contracting), and all bending/movement.
Muscular force can only be applied when the source (muscle) is in contact with the object.
FRICTION:

DEFINITION: Friction is the force responsible for changing the state of motion of objects in situations where no apparent force is acting. It acts in the direction OPPOSITE to the direction of motion.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A ball rolling on the ground gradually slows down and comes to rest due to friction.
When we stop pedalling a bicycle, it gradually slows down and stops due to friction.
A boat stops moving when we stop rowing due to friction with water.
The force of friction always acts on moving objects and is always opposite to the direction of motion.
Friction arises due to contact between surfaces - hence it is a contact force.

items.question: What is muscular force? Give one example.
items.answer:
The force resulting due to the action of muscles in our body is known as muscular force. It is a contact force because the muscles must be in contact with the object.
Example: Lifting a bucket of water from the ground - we use the muscular force of our arms and hands to lift it.

items.question: What is friction? State its direction with respect to motion.
items.answer:
Friction is the force responsible for changing the state of motion (slowing down or stopping) of moving objects. Friction arises due to contact between surfaces.
Direction: The force of friction always acts on moving objects in the direction OPPOSITE to the direction of their motion.
Example: A ball rolling on the ground experiences friction in the direction opposite to its rolling - this gradually slows it down.

items.question: Why are muscular force and friction both called contact forces?
items.answer:
Muscular force and friction are both contact forces because they can only act when there is physical contact between the agent (force-applying object) and the object on which the force acts.

Muscular force: Our muscles must be in contact with the object to push, lift, or pull it. For example, to push a table, our hands must touch the table. If we remove our hands, no muscular force acts on the table.

Friction: Friction arises due to contact between surfaces. For example, when a ball rolls on the ground, the surfaces of the ball and ground are in contact. This contact produces friction that opposes the motion. If there were no contact (e.g., a ball moving through outer space), there would be no friction.

Therefore, both forces require physical contact and are rightly called contact forces.

items.question: Explain the role of muscular force in the bodies of animals using examples.
items.answer:
Animals also make use of muscular force to carry out their physical activities and tasks.
Example 1: Bullocks are used to pull carts and ploughs in the field. The bullocks use their muscular force to pull the heavy loads.
Example 2: Horses, donkeys, and camels are used as pack animals. They use muscular force to carry heavy loads on their backs or to pull vehicles.
Example 3 (human body): Muscular force in the body enables digestion (muscles push food through the alimentary canal), breathing (muscles of the lungs expand and contract), and all movement of limbs.
These examples show that muscular force is not only used by humans but by all animals to perform tasks requiring motion, lifting, or carrying of loads.

items.question: "A ball rolling on the ground gradually slows down and finally comes to rest." What force is responsible for this? Describe its properties.
items.answer:
The force responsible for the ball gradually slowing down and coming to rest is FRICTION.

PROPERTIES OF FRICTION:
1. Direction: Friction always acts in the direction OPPOSITE to the direction of motion. The ball rolls forward, so friction acts backward on the ball.
2. Effect: Friction reduces the speed of moving objects. If friction is large enough, it brings the object to a complete stop.
3. Contact nature: Friction arises due to the contact between two surfaces - in this case, the surface of the ball and the surface of the ground. It is a contact force.
4. Always present: Friction acts on ALL moving objects (where surfaces are in contact). Other examples: when we stop pedalling a bicycle, it slows down due to friction; a boat stops when we stop rowing due to friction with water.
5. Cannot be avoided: As long as surfaces are in contact and an object moves, friction will always act opposing the motion.

items.question: What is the role of muscular force in the human body? Explain with at least three examples.
items.answer:
Muscular force is the force resulting from the action of muscles in our body. It plays a vital role in nearly all activities of the human body.

1. LIFTING AND CARRYING OBJECTS:
When we pick up a school bag or lift a bucket of water, our arm and shoulder muscles contract and apply a muscular force upward on the object to lift it against gravity.

2. DIGESTION:
During digestion, the food in the alimentary canal is pushed through by muscular force. The muscles lining the alimentary canal contract and relax in a wave-like motion (peristalsis) to push food forward. This is also a muscular force acting on the food inside the body.

3. BREATHING:
When we inhale, the muscles of the chest wall and the diaphragm contract and expand, increasing the chest volume so that air rushes into the lungs. When we exhale, these muscles relax and contract, pushing air out. Lungs expand and contract while we inhale and exhale - this is due to muscular force.

4. BODY MOVEMENT:
Every action we perform - walking, running, writing, eating - involves muscles contracting and relaxing to move our bones. The muscular force enables all voluntary and involuntary movements of the body.

CONCLUSION: Muscular force is a fundamental contact force that is responsible for virtually all physical activities performed by living beings - both inside and outside the body.

items.question: Explain with examples all the contact forces discussed in Chapter 8. Why are they called contact forces? How do muscular force and friction affect our daily lives?
items.answer:
CONTACT FORCES:
Contact forces are forces that act only when the agent applying the force is in direct physical contact with the object. If there is no contact, these forces cannot act.

Two main contact forces discussed in Chapter 8:

1. MUSCULAR FORCE:
DEFINITION: The force resulting from the action of muscles is called muscular force.
WHY IT IS A CONTACT FORCE: Muscles can exert force only when they are in contact with the object being moved. For example, to push a table, your hands must touch the table surface. The muscles in your arms apply force through your hands.
EXAMPLES IN DAILY LIFE:
- Pushing, pulling, lifting any object.
- Animals using muscular force: bullocks pulling plough, horses carrying loads (Fig. 8.9).
- Inside the body: food pushed through alimentary canal by muscles of digestive system.
- Breathing: muscles of lungs expand and contract to breathe.
- All movement: walking, running, writing are possible due to muscular force.

2. FRICTION:
DEFINITION: Friction is the contact force that opposes the motion of moving objects. It acts between surfaces in contact, always in the direction opposite to motion.
WHY IT IS A CONTACT FORCE: Friction exists because of the contact between two surfaces. Without contact, friction cannot exist. For example, a ball rolling in outer space (no surface contact) would not experience friction.
EXAMPLES IN DAILY LIFE:
- A rolling ball on the ground gradually slows down and stops due to friction.
- A bicycle gradually slows down when pedalling is stopped - friction between tyres and road, and within the bicycle mechanism.
- A boat stops when rowing is stopped - friction between boat and water.
- Writing on paper is possible because of friction between pen/pencil and paper.
- Walking is possible because friction between shoe and ground prevents slipping.

EFFECT ON DAILY LIFE:
Muscular force enables all voluntary activities - moving, lifting, sport, and even internal bodily functions. Without muscular force, no movement would be possible.
Friction, while it slows objects down (which can be disadvantageous), also makes walking, writing, and braking possible (advantageous). Life would be impossible without friction - we could not walk or hold objects.

SUMMARY: Both muscular force and friction are contact forces that play essential roles in our daily lives. Muscular force enables motion and function; friction controls and often enables that motion safely.

sections.text: Non-contact forces are forces that can act on an object without being in physical contact with it. These forces act from a distance.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Three types of non-contact forces:
1. MAGNETIC FORCE
2. ELECTROSTATIC FORCE
3. GRAVITATIONAL FORCE
MAGNETIC FORCE:
DEFINITION: The force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or on magnetic materials (like iron) is called magnetic force.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Like poles of two magnets REPEL each other (push away).
Unlike poles of two magnets ATTRACT each other (pull towards).
A magnet can exert force on another magnet WITHOUT being in contact with it.
Both attraction and repulsion can occur without contact - hence non-contact force.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.6:
sections.aim: To observe attraction and repulsion between magnets without contact.
sections.materials: Two bar magnets, three round pencils or wooden rollers.
procedure: Step 1: Place one magnet on three rollers. Bring one end of the second magnet near the same end of the first. Observe what happens.
Step 2: Bring the OTHER end of the second magnet near the same end of the first. Observe what happens.
sections.observation:
- Same ends (like poles) brought near: First magnet moves AWAY (repulsion).
- Opposite ends (unlike poles) brought near: First magnet moves TOWARD the approaching magnet (attraction).
sections.conclusion:
A magnet can exert a force on another magnet from a distance (without contact). This force may be attraction or repulsion depending on which poles are brought near each other. Magnetic force is a non-contact force.

ELECTROSTATIC FORCE:
DEFINITION: The force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body is known as electrostatic force. It is also a non-contact force.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A charged body is one that has acquired electric charge (e.g., a straw rubbed with paper).
A straw rubbed with paper attracts another straw that has NOT been rubbed (attraction between charged and uncharged bodies).
A straw rubbed with paper REPELS another straw that has also been rubbed with paper (repulsion between like charges).
Electrostatic force operates even when the bodies are not in contact.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.7:
sections.aim: To observe attraction and repulsion due to electrostatic force.
sections.materials: Two plastic straws, thread, piece of paper.
procedure: Step 1: Cut a plastic straw into two equal pieces. Suspend one piece from the edge of a table with a thread.
Step 2: Rub the free end of the suspended piece with a sheet of paper. Bring the other piece (NOT rubbed) near it. Observe.
Step 3: Rub the free end of the second piece with paper. Now bring this rubbed end near the rubbed end of the suspended straw. Observe.
sections.observation:
(Fig. 8.11):
- Rubbed straw brought near unrubbed straw: ATTRACTION (straw is pulled toward it).
- Rubbed straw brought near another rubbed straw: REPULSION (straw is pushed away).
sections.conclusion:
Electrostatic force can be attraction (between oppositely charged objects) or repulsion (between like charged objects). It acts without contact - hence it is a non-contact force. Charged bodies exert electrostatic force.

GRAVITATIONAL FORCE:
DEFINITION: Every object in the universe exerts a force of attraction on every other object. This force is known as the gravitational force.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Objects fall to the ground when released because the earth pulls them (gravity).
The force of gravity acts on ALL objects everywhere - whether on earth or in the universe.
Gravity acts without physical contact - it is a non-contact force.
The force of gravity acts on all objects all the time without our being aware of it.
Water flows downward and rivers flow toward the sea due to gravity.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (Do you know box):
sections.text:
Gravity is not a property of the earth alone. Every object in the universe - whether small or large - exerts a force of attraction on every other object. This force is known as the gravitational force.

items.question: What is gravitational force? Why is it a non-contact force?
items.answer:
The force of attraction exerted by the earth (or any object) on all other objects is called gravitational force or gravity.
It is a non-contact force because the earth attracts objects (like falling fruits from a tree, water flowing down, a coin falling from your hand) without being in direct contact with them. Gravity acts from a distance - the earth does not need to touch an object for gravity to pull it.

The magnets are NOT in contact during the activity, yet the first magnet moves due to the force exerted by the second magnet from a distance.
sections.conclusion:

Q5[4 Marks] What is gravitational force? Why does every object in the universe attract every other object?
A5:
GRAVITATIONAL FORCE:
Every object in the universe exerts a force of attraction on every other object. This force is called gravitational force.

On Earth:
- When a coin slips from your hand, it falls to the ground. The earth pulls it down. This pull is the force of gravity.
- Leaves and fruits fall from plants when they detach - gravity pulls them down.
- Water flows from a tap toward the ground as soon as the tap is opened - due to gravity.
- Rivers flow downward toward the sea - due to gravity.

Universal Nature:
Gravity is NOT a property of the earth alone. Every object in the universe - whether small or large, whether it is a planet, star, or tiny particle - exerts a gravitational force of attraction on every other object. This was stated by Isaac Newton.
Example: The sun's gravitational force holds the planets in their orbits. The moon's gravitational force causes tides on earth.

Why NON-CONTACT?
Gravitational force acts from a distance. The earth pulls a falling apple without touching it. The sun pulls the earth across millions of kilometres of empty space. This is why gravitational force is a non-contact force.

Q6[4 Marks] Distinguish between contact forces and non-contact forces. Give two examples of each with explanation.
A6:
CONTACT FORCES:
Definition: Forces that act only when the agent is in direct physical contact with the object.
Examples:
1. Muscular force: A person lifting a table must touch the table with their hands. Muscles in the hands and arms apply force directly on the table through contact.
2. Friction: Friction between a rolling ball and the ground arises because the surfaces of the ball and ground are in contact. Without contact, no friction.

NON-CONTACT FORCES:
Definition: Forces that can act on objects from a distance, without physical contact between the agent and the object.
Examples:
1. Magnetic force (Activity 8.6): One magnet placed on rollers moves when another magnet is brought near it - even without the two magnets touching. The force acts across the gap between them.
2. Gravitational force: The earth attracts a falling coin from a distance - the earth does not touch the coin, yet pulls it downward through gravitational force.

KEY DIFFERENCE:
Contact forces require physical touching (agent must touch the object). Non-contact forces act across empty space (no touching required). Both are real forces and can change the state of motion or shape of objects.

sections.text:
Pressure is the force acting per unit area of a surface.
FORMULA: Pressure = Force / Area on which it acts

points: Force and pressure are related: the same force produces MORE pressure on a SMALLER area, and LESS pressure on a LARGER area.
Area is in the DENOMINATOR: smaller area = larger pressure for the same force.
Sharp tools (knife, nail, needle) cut/pierce better because their pointed end has VERY SMALL AREA, producing very large pressure for the same force.
Shoulder bags with broad straps are more comfortable than thin straps because a broad strap distributes force over a larger area, reducing pressure on the shoulder.
Tools for cutting and piercing always have sharp edges (small area) to produce maximum pressure.
A porter places a round cloth pad on the head to carry heavy loads - this increases the area of contact, reducing pressure on the head.

sections.label: FORMULA:
items: Pressure = Force / Area on which it acts
- SI Unit of Pressure: Pascal (Pa) where 1 Pa = 1 N/m2
- Note: Only forces perpendicular (at right angles) to the surface are considered when calculating pressure on that surface.
WORKED EXAMPLE:
A force of 50 N acts on an area of 10 m2.
Pressure = Force / Area = 50 / 10 = 5 Pa
WHY SHARP TOOLS ARE BETTER:

A nail has a pointed tip with very small area. When you push a nail by its pointed end, the force acts over this tiny area, producing very large pressure - enough to penetrate wood. If you try to push a nail by its blunt head, the same force is spread over a larger area, producing less pressure - not enough to penetrate wood.

items.question: Why do cutting tools have sharp edges?
items.answer: Cutting tools have sharp edges because a sharp edge has a very small area. According to the formula Pressure = Force / Area, for a given force, smaller area means greater pressure. The large pressure at the sharp edge is sufficient to cut through materials. A blunt edge has a larger area, producing less pressure for the same force, making cutting difficult.

items.question: A porter places a round cloth pad on his head before carrying a heavy load. Explain why, using the concept of pressure.
items.answer:
When a porter carries a heavy load on his head, the weight of the load (a downward force) acts on the contact area between the load and the head.
- Without the cloth pad: The load contacts the head over a small area, producing LARGE PRESSURE on the head, causing pain.
- With the round cloth pad: The cloth pad increases the area of contact between the load and the head. According to Pressure = Force / Area, the same force (weight of load) now acts over a LARGER AREA, resulting in SMALLER PRESSURE on the head.
- This reduced pressure makes it easier and less painful for the porter to carry the load.

items.question: Why is it easier to drive a nail into wood using its pointed end rather than its flat head?
items.answer:
Using the POINTED end:
- The pointed tip of a nail has a very small area.
- Pressure = Force / Area. For the same applied force, the very small area at the pointed tip produces VERY LARGE PRESSURE.
- This large pressure is sufficient to push the nail into the wood.

Using the FLAT HEAD:
- The flat head has a much larger area than the pointed tip.
- For the same applied force, the larger area produces MUCH LESS PRESSURE.
- This smaller pressure is insufficient to penetrate the wood.

Therefore, it is far easier to drive a nail using the pointed end. This principle is used in all tools meant for cutting, piercing, or penetrating - they always have sharp, small-area ends (knives, needles, pins, drills) to maximize pressure for a given applied force.

items.question: What is pressure? Calculate the pressure when a force of 100 N acts on an area of 25 m2. Also calculate the pressure when the same force acts on an area of 5 m2. What do you observe?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Pressure is the force acting per unit area of a surface.
FORMULA: Pressure = Force / Area on which it acts
UNIT: Pascal (Pa) = N/m2

CALCULATION 1 (Area = 25 m2):
Pressure = Force / Area
Pressure = 100 / 25
Pressure = 4 Pa

CALCULATION 2 (Area = 5 m2):
Pressure = Force / Area
Pressure = 100 / 5
Pressure = 20 Pa

OBSERVATION:
The same force of 100 N produces DIFFERENT pressures on DIFFERENT areas.
- On 25 m2: Pressure = 4 Pa (SMALLER pressure on LARGER area)
- On 5 m2: Pressure = 20 Pa (LARGER pressure on SMALLER area)
CONCLUSION: For a given force, as area DECREASES, pressure INCREASES. As area INCREASES, pressure DECREASES. Area is in the denominator of the pressure formula, which explains this inverse relationship between area and pressure.

Q6[4 Marks] Explain why shoulder bags with broad straps are more comfortable than those with thin straps. Use the concept of pressure.
A6:
When we carry a shoulder bag, the strap exerts a downward force (weight of the bag) on our shoulder. The discomfort depends on the PRESSURE exerted on the shoulder.

PRESSURE = FORCE / AREA

For a THIN strap:
The contact area between the thin strap and the shoulder is SMALL.
For the same weight of the bag (same force), a smaller area means: LARGER PRESSURE on the shoulder.
This large pressure causes pain and discomfort.

For a BROAD strap:
The contact area between the broad strap and the shoulder is LARGE.
For the same weight of the bag (same force), a larger area means: SMALLER PRESSURE on the shoulder.
This small pressure causes less pain and discomfort.

CONCLUSION:
Broad straps distribute the force over a larger area, reducing the pressure on the shoulder and making the bag more comfortable to carry. This is why designers use wide shoulder straps on heavy bags. The same principle explains why backpack straps are made broad and padded.

Q7[6 Marks] Write a comprehensive note on pressure - its definition, formula, unit, and how the area of contact affects pressure. Include examples from Activity in the chapter and daily life.
A7:
PRESSURE:

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Pressure is the force acting per unit area of a surface. When a force acts on an object, the effect it produces (its ability to penetrate, cut, or press into a surface) depends not only on the magnitude of the force but also on the area over which it acts.

sections.label: FORMULA:
items: Pressure = Force / Area on which it acts
Or, P = F / A
where P = Pressure, F = Force, A = Area.
UNIT:
The SI unit of pressure is Pascal (Pa).
1 Pa = 1 N/m2 (one Newton per square metre).
Pressure is force per unit area.
NOTE: Only forces perpendicular (at right angles) to the surface are considered when calculating pressure.
HOW AREA AFFECTS PRESSURE:
From the formula P = F / A:
- For a FIXED force, if area DECREASES, pressure INCREASES (area and pressure are inversely related).
- For a FIXED force, if area INCREASES, pressure DECREASES.
EXAMPLES FROM THE CHAPTER:
1. Sharp nail vs blunt head (Fig. 8.12):
Pushing a nail by its pointed end into wood: The pointed tip has very small area. Same applied force → very large pressure at tip → nail penetrates wood easily.
Pushing a nail by its flat head: Larger area → smaller pressure → nail does not penetrate wood.
2. Porter carrying heavy load (Fig. 8.13 and Paheli's observation):
Without cloth pad: Load contacts head over small area → large pressure → pain.
With round cloth pad: Increases area of contact → smaller pressure → easier to carry.
3. Broad vs thin shoulder strap:
Thin strap: small area → large pressure on shoulder → painful.
Broad strap: large area → small pressure on shoulder → comfortable.
4. Sharp knife vs blunt knife:
Sharp knife: very small edge area → large pressure → cuts vegetables easily.
Blunt knife: larger edge area → small pressure → cutting is difficult.
5. Camel's feet:
Camels have very broad, flat feet. This large area reduces pressure on sand, preventing them from sinking in - an adaptation to desert conditions.
GENERAL CONCLUSION:

Pressure depends on both the force applied and the area over which it acts. Increasing the area for the same force reduces pressure. Decreasing the area for the same force increases pressure. This principle is used in the design of many tools and everyday objects to either maximize (cutting tools, needles) or minimize (furniture legs, snowshoes, camel feet) pressure.

topics.topic_name: PRESSURE EXERTED BY LIQUIDS AND GASES

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Liquids and gases exert pressure on all surfaces in contact with them, including the walls of their containers.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Liquids exert pressure on the WALLS and the BOTTOM of their containers.
The pressure exerted by a liquid at the BOTTOM of the container is due to the weight of the liquid above.
Pressure increases with DEPTH: deeper parts of a liquid are under greater pressure.
Liquids exert pressure in ALL DIRECTIONS at the same depth (not just downward).
Gases also exert pressure on the walls of their containers (e.g., inflated balloon, bicycle tyre).
Gases exert pressure in ALL DIRECTIONS on the walls of their containers.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.8:
sections.aim: To observe that liquid exerts pressure on the bottom and walls of a container.
sections.materials: A transparent glass tube (25 cm long, 5-7.5 cm diameter), thin rubber sheet (from a balloon), water.
procedure: Step 1: Stretch a rubber sheet tightly over one end of the glass tube. Hold the tube vertically.
Step 2: Ask a friend to pour water into the tube. Observe the rubber sheet.
Step 3: Pour more water. Observe again.
Step 4: Try to see if there is any relation between the bulge in the rubber sheet and the height of the water column.
sections.observation: As more water is added, the rubber sheet at the bottom bulges more outward. The higher the water column (height), the greater the bulge.
sections.conclusion: The water exerts pressure on the rubber sheet at the bottom. This pressure increases with the height (depth) of the water column. Liquids exert pressure on the bottom of their containers.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.9:
sections.aim: To observe that liquid exerts pressure on the SIDES (walls) of a container.
sections.materials: A plastic bottle, a cylindrical glass tube (few cm long), rubber sheet, molten wax, water.
procedure: Step 1: Fix a short glass tube near the bottom of a plastic bottle using heated glass (seal with molten wax to prevent leakage).
Step 2: Cover the mouth of the glass tube with a thin rubber sheet (as in Activity 8.8).
Step 3: Fill the bottle with water up to half.
sections.observation: The rubber sheet fixed to the SIDE of the bottle bulges outward (even though the rubber sheet is on the side, not the bottom).
sections.conclusion: Water exerts pressure not only on the BOTTOM but also on the SIDES (walls) of the container. Liquids exert pressure on the walls of the container.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.10:
sections.aim: To observe that liquid exerts equal pressure at the same depth in all directions.
sections.materials: A plastic bottle, drill/punch, water.
procedure: Step 1: Take a plastic bottle. Drill four holes all around the bottle near its bottom at the same height.
Step 2: Fill the bottle with water.
sections.observation: (Fig. 8.16): Water streams come out of all four holes. The streams fall at the SAME DISTANCE from the bottle. The holes are at the same depth, and the streams are equal in pressure.
sections.conclusion:
Gases also exert pressure on the walls of their containers. This pressure acts in all directions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Do liquids exert pressure only on the bottom of the container? Explain.
items.answer:
No, liquids do not exert pressure only on the bottom. Liquids exert pressure on the BOTTOM as well as on the SIDES (walls) of the container.
Activity 8.9 demonstrates this: when the rubber sheet is fixed on the SIDE of a bottle filled with water, it bulges outward. This shows that water exerts pressure sideways on the walls, not just downward on the bottom.

items.question: What does Activity 8.10 demonstrate about the pressure exerted by liquids?
items.answer:
Activity 8.10 demonstrates that liquids exert EQUAL PRESSURE at the same DEPTH in all directions (not just downward).
When four holes are drilled at the same height around a water-filled bottle, the water streams come out of all four holes and fall at the SAME DISTANCE from the bottle. This means the pressure at the same depth is equal in all directions (front, back, left, right), proving that liquids exert pressure equally at the same depth in all directions.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.8. What does the bulging rubber sheet indicate?

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.8 - Pressure at the Bottom of a Liquid:
sections.materials: Glass tube (~25 cm long), thin rubber sheet, water.
procedure: Step 1: Stretch a rubber sheet tightly over one end of the glass tube. Hold it vertically (rubber sheet at the bottom).
Step 2: Pour some water into the open top of the tube. Observe the rubber sheet.
Step 3: Pour more water. Observe again.
sections.observation:
The rubber sheet at the bottom bulges outward. As more water is added (greater height of water column), the rubber sheet bulges MORE.

WHAT THE BULGE INDICATES:
The rubber sheet is being pushed outward by a force. This force is the pressure exerted by the water on the rubber sheet at the bottom. The greater the height (depth) of water above, the greater the weight of water pressing down, and the greater the pressure on the rubber sheet at the bottom.
sections.conclusion:
Liquids exert pressure on the bottom of their containers, and this pressure increases with the depth (height) of the liquid above.

Q4[3 Marks] Explain why water gushes out strongly when a hole is made near the bottom of a full container.
A4:
When a hole is made near the BOTTOM of a full container of water:
1. The water at the bottom is under GREATER PRESSURE than water near the top.
2. This is because there is a larger column of water above (greater depth), and the weight of all that water above creates higher pressure at the bottom.
3. According to Activity 8.8, pressure increases with depth.
4. When a hole is made near the bottom, the water is forced out by this large pressure. The greater the pressure (i.e., the deeper the hole), the faster and stronger the water gushes out.
5. A hole made near the top would have less water above it (smaller depth), less pressure, so water would flow out more slowly.
This is why engineers consider pressure when designing dams, pipelines, and water tanks - the walls near the bottom must be stronger to withstand higher pressure.

Q5[4 Marks] Describe Activity 8.9. What does it prove about pressure exerted by liquids?
A5:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.9 - Pressure on Walls of a Container:
sections.materials: Plastic bottle, short cylindrical glass tube, rubber sheet, molten wax, water.
procedure: Step 1: Fix a short glass tube near the BOTTOM of a plastic bottle (make a hole in the side, insert the glass tube). Seal the joint with molten wax to prevent leakage.
Step 2: Cover the open mouth of the glass tube with a thin rubber sheet (as in Activity 8.8).
Step 3: Fill the bottle with water up to half its height.
Step 4: Observe the rubber sheet on the side of the bottle.
sections.observation:
The rubber sheet fixed on the SIDE (wall) of the bottle bulges outward. As the bottle is filled with more water, the bulge increases.

WHAT IT PROVES:
The rubber sheet is on the SIDE of the bottle, not the bottom. Its outward bulge means that a force is pushing it outward from inside. This force is the PRESSURE exerted by the liquid (water) on the SIDE WALL of the container.
sections.conclusion:
Gases, like liquids, exert pressure on the walls of their containers. This pressure acts in ALL directions. This is the basis of many technologies: bicycle tyres, air-filled footballs, inflatable structures, and gas storage cylinders all depend on the pressure of gases.

Q7[6 Marks] Describe all three activities (8.8, 8.9, 8.10) related to pressure exerted by liquids and gases. What do these activities collectively prove?
A7:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.8 - Pressure at the Bottom of Liquid:
sections.materials:
Glass tube, rubber sheet, water.
KEY PROCEDURE: Rubber sheet stretched over the bottom of a glass tube. Water poured in from top.
KEY OBSERVATION: Rubber sheet bulges outward at the bottom. More water (greater height) = more bulge.
sections.conclusion: Liquid exerts pressure on the BOTTOM of the container. Pressure increases with depth (height of liquid above).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.9 - Pressure on the Walls of a Container:
sections.materials:
Plastic bottle, short glass tube fixed to side, rubber sheet, water.
KEY PROCEDURE: Rubber sheet fixed on the SIDE of the bottle. Bottle filled with water.
KEY OBSERVATION: Rubber sheet on the side of the bottle bulges outward.
sections.conclusion: Liquid exerts pressure on the SIDE WALLS of the container, not just the bottom.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.10 - Equal Pressure at the Same Depth:
sections.materials:
Plastic bottle with four holes at equal heights, water.
KEY PROCEDURE: Four holes drilled at the same height all around the bottle. Bottle filled with water.
KEY OBSERVATION (Fig. 8.16): Water streams emerge from all four holes and fall at the SAME DISTANCE from the bottle.
sections.conclusion:
Liquids exert pressure on walls of containers.

COLLECTIVE CONCLUSION FROM ALL ACTIVITIES:
1. Liquids exert pressure on the BOTTOM of their containers (Activity 8.8).
2. Liquids exert pressure on the WALLS (sides) of their containers (Activity 8.9).
3. Liquids exert EQUAL pressure at the SAME DEPTH in ALL DIRECTIONS (Activity 8.10).
4. Gases also exert pressure on the walls of their containers in all directions.
5. Overall: Liquids and gases exert pressure on all surfaces in contact with them.
This is a fundamental property of fluids (liquids and gases) - they exert pressure in all directions, unlike solids which exert pressure mainly downward.
