sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The pressure exerted by the air (atmosphere) surrounding us on all objects is called atmospheric pressure.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The earth is surrounded by a layer of air called the ATMOSPHERE.
The atmospheric air extends up to many kilometres above the surface of the earth.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a unit area pressing down on the surface.
Atmospheric pressure is very large - we do not feel it because the pressure inside our bodies is also equal to the atmospheric pressure and balances it.
Atmospheric pressure = force of gravity on the air in a column of unit area above that point.
Atmospheric pressure acts in ALL directions - downward, upward, and sideways.
ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE FORMULA (conceptual):

If we imagine a unit area on the earth's surface with a very long cylinder of air standing on it (extending to the top of the atmosphere), the atmospheric pressure = force of gravity on all the air in that cylinder.
MAGNITUDE OF ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE:

The area of a person's head is approximately 15 cm x 15 cm. The force due to the atmospheric air on a 15 cm x 15 cm area is nearly equal to the force of gravity on an object of mass 225 kg (2250 N). This is the magnitude of atmospheric pressure.
We do not feel this force because the pressure inside our bodies is also equal to the atmospheric pressure - the two pressures balance each other.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.11:
sections.aim: To observe the effect of atmospheric pressure using a rubber sucker.
sections.materials: A good quality rubber sucker (small rubber cup).
procedure: Step 1: Take a rubber sucker (looks like a small rubber cup - Fig. 8.18).
Step 2: Press it hard on a smooth flat surface (table, wall, glass).
Step 3: Try to pull it off the surface.
sections.observation:
When pressed, the sucker sticks firmly to the surface. It is very difficult to pull it off.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION:
- When the sucker is pressed onto the surface, most of the air between the rubber cup and the surface is pushed out.
- Now the atmospheric air is pressing the outer surface of the sucker (pushing it toward the surface).
- The pressure of the atmosphere acts on the sucker from outside, pressing it firmly against the surface.
- To pull the sucker off, you need to apply a force large enough to overcome the atmospheric pressure.
sections.conclusion: The sucker sticks because atmospheric pressure acts on its outer surface. Atmospheric pressure is very large - equal to about 2250 N on a 15 cm x 15 cm area.

sections.label: DO YOU KNOW BOX (Otto von Guericke Experiment):
sections.text:
Otto von Guericke, a German scientist of the 17th century, invented a pump to extract air out of a vessel. He demonstrated dramatically the force of air pressure. He joined two hollow metallic hemispheres of 51 cm diameter each and pumped air out of them. Then he employed EIGHT HORSES on each hemisphere (16 horses total) to pull them apart (Fig. 8.20). So great is the force of air pressure that the hemispheres could not be pulled apart - even with 16 horses pulling from opposite sides.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is atmospheric pressure?
items.answer: The pressure exerted by the air (atmosphere) surrounding us on all objects is called atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is the envelope of air surrounding the earth. Atmospheric pressure is the force of gravity on the air in a column of unit area extending from that point up to the top of the atmosphere.

items.question: Why do we not feel the large atmospheric pressure acting on our bodies?
items.answer: We do not feel the large atmospheric pressure acting on our bodies because the pressure inside our bodies is also equal to the atmospheric pressure. The internal pressure of our bodies balances (equals) the atmospheric pressure from outside. Since the two pressures are equal and opposite, there is no net pressure difference, and we do not feel crushed.

items.question: Describe Activity 8.11 and explain why the rubber sucker sticks to a surface.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.11 - Rubber Sucker and Atmospheric Pressure:
sections.materials: A rubber sucker (small rubber cup).
procedure: 1: He joined two hollow metallic hemispheres (half-spheres) of 51 cm diameter each together to form a complete sphere.
Step 2: He used his air pump to remove all (or most) the air from inside the joined sphere, creating a near-vacuum.
Step 3: He then attached EIGHT HORSES to each hemisphere (sixteen horses total - eight pulling each half in opposite directions) and tried to pull the two hemispheres apart.
RESULT: Despite 16 horses pulling, the two hemispheres could not be separated.
DEMONSTRATION:

The two hemispheres were held together by atmospheric pressure acting from outside. Since the inside was a vacuum (no air pressure), the outside atmospheric pressure pressed the two hemispheres together with enormous force.
sections.observation:
The sucker sticks firmly to the surface. It is very difficult to pull off.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION:
When the rubber sucker is pressed hard, most air between the rubber cup and the surface escapes out.
Now the atmospheric air (outside) presses the sucker against the surface from all sides.
The atmospheric pressure acts on the outer curved surface of the sucker, pushing it firmly toward the surface.
To pull the sucker off, you must apply a force greater than the atmospheric pressure acting on the sucker's area.
sections.conclusion: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a unit area. It is very large (~2250 N on a 15 cm x 15 cm area) but we do not feel it because our internal body pressure equals atmospheric pressure. Otto von Guericke's experiment and the rubber sucker activity both demonstrate the large magnitude of atmospheric pressure.

sections.label: EXERCISE 5: In the following situations, identify the agent exerting the force and the object on which it acts. State the effect of the force in each case:
sections.raw:
(a) Squeezing a piece of lemon between the fingers to extract its juice.
(b) Taking out paste from a toothpaste tube.
(c) A load suspended from a spring while its other end is on a hook fixed to a wall.
(d) An athlete making a high jump to clear the bar at a certain height.

ANSWERS:
(a) Agent: Fingers / Muscular force of the person.
Object: The piece of lemon.
Effect: Force changes the shape of the lemon - it squeezes and juice comes out.

(b) Agent: Fingers/hands of the person (muscular force).
Object: The toothpaste tube.
Effect: Force changes the shape of the tube - it is squeezed and paste is pushed out.

(c) Agent: Gravitational force (gravity) / Weight of the load.
Object: The spring.
Effect: Force changes the shape of the spring - it stretches (elongates).

(d) Agent: Muscular force of the athlete's legs.
Object: The ground (reaction) and the athlete's own body.
Effect: Muscular force on the ground gives a reaction force that propels the athlete upward (change in state of motion - from rest/running to jumping upward).

EXERCISE 6: A blacksmith hammers a hot piece of iron while making a tool. How does the force due to hammering affect the piece of iron?
EXERCISE ANSWER:
A blacksmith hammers a hot piece of iron with great force. The hammer hits the iron piece repeatedly with large force. Since the iron piece is not free to move (it is placed on an anvil), the force causes a CHANGE IN SHAPE of the iron piece - it is flattened, bent, or given a particular shape. The force due to hammering changes the shape of the iron piece. This is an example of force changing the shape of an object (as demonstrated in Activity 8.5 and Table 8.2).

EXERCISE 7: An inflated balloon was pressed against a wall after it had been rubbed with a piece of synthetic cloth. It was found that the balloon sticks to the wall. What force might be responsible for the attraction between the balloon and the wall?
EXERCISE ANSWER:
When the balloon is rubbed with synthetic cloth, it acquires an ELECTRIC CHARGE (electrostatic charge). This charged balloon, when pressed against the wall, exerts an ELECTROSTATIC FORCE of attraction on the wall (which is uncharged or develops opposite charge on its surface). This electrostatic force of attraction holds the balloon against the wall. The force responsible is ELECTROSTATIC FORCE - a non-contact force exerted by charged bodies on other charged or uncharged bodies.

EXERCISE 8: Name the forces acting on a plastic bucket containing water held above the ground level in your hand. Discuss why the forces acting on the bucket do not bring a change in its state of motion.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
FORCES ACTING ON THE BUCKET:
1. Gravitational force (gravity) - The earth pulls the bucket and the water inside it DOWNWARD.
2. Muscular force - The person holding the bucket applies a muscular force UPWARD on the bucket through their hand.

WHY NO CHANGE IN STATE OF MOTION:
The bucket is at rest (state of rest = zero speed).
For the state of motion to change, there must be a NET force on the bucket.
- Gravity pulls the bucket DOWNWARD.
- Muscular force pushes the bucket UPWARD.
- Both forces are EQUAL IN MAGNITUDE and OPPOSITE IN DIRECTION.
- Net force = Gravity - Muscular force = 0 (they cancel each other out).
Since the net force on the bucket is zero, there is no change in its state of motion - it remains at rest (in the hand, above the ground).

EXERCISE 9: A rocket has been fired upwards to launch a satellite in its orbit. Name the two forces acting on the rocket immediately after leaving the launching pad.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Two forces acting on the rocket immediately after leaving the launching pad:
1. GRAVITATIONAL FORCE (Force of Gravity): The earth exerts a gravitational pull on the rocket in the DOWNWARD direction, trying to pull the rocket back toward earth.
2. FORCE OF FRICTION (due to air): As the rocket moves upward through the atmosphere at high speed, air exerts a frictional force on the rocket in the DOWNWARD direction (opposing the upward motion).
(Note: The thrust of the rocket engine is the force that propels it upward, but the question asks for forces acting ON the rocket from outside - gravity and air friction are the two main external forces.)

sections.label: EXERCISE 10: When we press the bulb of a dropper with its nozzle kept in water, air in the dropper is seen to escape in the form of bubbles. Once we release the pressure on the bulb, water gets filled in the dropper. The rise of water in the dropper is due to:
sections.raw:
(a) pressure of water
(b) gravity of the earth
(c) shape of rubber bulb
(d) atmospheric pressure
EXERCISE ANSWER: (d) atmospheric pressure

ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: When the bulb is squeezed, air escapes as bubbles from the nozzle. Now the inside of the dropper has less air (lower pressure). When the pressure is released, the outside atmospheric pressure (which is greater than the pressure inside the dropper) pushes the water upward through the nozzle and into the dropper. The water rises into the dropper because atmospheric pressure acts on the water surface outside and pushes it into the region of lower pressure inside the dropper.
